442.title: Ashtpadi 2, salok: destroyer of pain
442.hook: deen darad dukh bhanjanaa: He destroys the pain of the humble (Sukhmani 2)
442.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the second ashtpadi, and some say it, or the whole bani, for someone who is ill or suffering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat, and your line: begin with remembering. When your reminder went off, did you stop for a breath? Today, the second ashtpadi opens. Day four hundred forty-two.

There's a kind of pain that doesn't make the news. The person who lost their job and hasn't told anyone yet. The old man whose children call twice a year. The new immigrant who can't read the letters arriving in the mail. Nobody is standing up for them. They don't have someone to ring, a cousin who knows someone, a name that opens doors. In Guru Arjan's Punjab there were words for people like that, and the second ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens by naming them, and naming who stands with them.
screen: `PAIN THAT DOESN'T MAKE THE NEWS.` → `NO ONE TO RING.` → `ASHTPADI 2 NAMES THEM.`

segments.voice: Here is the salok: deen darad dukh bhanjanaa, ghat ghat naath anaath. Word by word. Deen: the poor, the humble, the ones with nothing to bargain with. Darad: pain, the ache that won't go away. Dukh: suffering, sorrow, the opposite of the sukh in Sukhmani. Bhanjanaa: the breaker, the one who smashes it to pieces. So: the One who breaks the pain and suffering of the humble. Then: ghat ghat naath: master of every heart, every single body. Then anaath, and here readers differ. Some translators take it as another name for God: the One with no master above. Others read naath anaath together: master of the masterless. In everyday Punjabi an anaath is an orphan, someone with no one, and on that reading the One is the protector of those with no protector. The second line of the salok is Nanak's own voice. In paraphrase: I have come to Your shelter; God, be with Nanak. Notice two things. First, the salok doesn't say pain never comes. It says there's a breaker of pain, and it names the people the breaker stands with: not the powerful, but the humble, and on one reading the unprotected. Second, look where the Guru puts himself. Not above the deen, but among them. He comes to the shelter too. That's the posture of the whole second ashtpadi. In the days ahead its stanzas will walk into the hardest places a person goes, places where no family can follow. But it begins here, with a name for God that anyone in pain can call on: the one who breaks it.
screen: `DEEN, DARAD, DUKH: THE HUMBLE'S PAIN.` · `BHANJANAA: THE ONE WHO BREAKS IT.` · `NAATH, ANAATH: TWO READINGS.` · `NANAK COMES TO THE SHELTER TOO.` · then, large: `HE BREAKS PAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone in pain. Or, if prayer isn't your practice, hold them in mind. Let one person come to you, someone whose pain you know about, or someone you sense has no one to ring. See them as clearly as you can. If you pray, you can say the salok's first words for them, deen darad dukh bhanjanaa, or simply Waheguru. If you don't, wish them one thing: that the pain breaks, a little. Stay with them for a while. The bell holds the time.
Dukh, suffering: Sukhmani's second section, whose salok names God the breaker of the pain of the humble and the master of every heart.
Your line: he breaks pain. Today, find one person who might have no one to ring, and be the one who rings, even for two minutes. Day four hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 442 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE NO FAMILY CAN GO.`

443.title: Where no family can go
443.hook: where no mother, father, child or friend can go, the Name goes with you (Sukhmani 2)
443.tomorrow: The Name on the hard road
443.howItsDone: Some Sikh families read this stanza, or the whole of Sukhmani, at the bedside of someone who is ill or dying.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dukh, and your line: he breaks pain, the protector of those with no protector. Did you ring someone who had no one to ring? Today, the first stanza. Day four hundred forty-three.

A hospital corridor, late. A family has walked with someone as far as they can: the parking lot, the waiting room, the double doors marked staff only. Then a nurse gently says, this is as far as you go. The doors swing shut. Everyone who loves the patient is standing on the wrong side. There are places a person has to go without the people who love them. The second ashtpadi's first stanza walks right up to that door.
screen: `A HOSPITAL CORRIDOR, LATE.` → `THIS IS AS FAR AS YOU GO.` → `THE DOORS SWING SHUT.`

segments.voice: Here is how the stanza begins, in paraphrase: where there is no mother, no father, no children, no friends, no brother, there, O mind, the Name goes with you as your help. The opening words are jah maat pitaa sut meet na bhaaee: where no mother, father, son, friend or brother. A person's closest ties, named one by one, and then set down at the door. Then the stanza goes on into harder places still. In paraphrase: where the great and terrible messenger of death would crush you, there only the Name goes along with you. Where the difficulty is very heavy, the Name of God saves you in an instant. Notice what the stanza is not saying. It isn't saying your family doesn't matter, or that love is useless. Sikh teaching honors the householder's life, the life of family and work. The stanza is pointing at something plainer: there are rooms other people can't enter with you. The operating room. The last hours of a life. And, in the stanza's own picture, the meeting with the messenger of death. In every one of those rooms, the stanza says, there is a companion who doesn't stop at the door. Read at a bedside, the stanza doesn't say the family isn't enough. It says the family can't go everywhere, and in the stanza's words, the Name can.
screen: `NO MOTHER, FATHER, CHILD OR FRIEND.` · `THE NAME GOES WITH YOU AS HELP.` · `ROOMS OTHERS CAN'T ENTER.` · `A COMPANION PAST THE DOOR.` · then, large: `THE NAME GOES TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with who goes with you. Close your eyes if that's comfortable. Picture the people who walk with you as far as they can: family, friends, whoever they are for you. Let yourself be grateful for each one. Then picture a door they can't come through, and you stepping through it, alone. Notice how that feels. Now, if you pray, say Waheguru, and imagine the Name stepping through the door with you. If you don't, simply notice your own breath, which also comes with you everywhere. The bell holds the time.
Naam, the Name: the first stanza of Sukhmani's second ashtpadi, where no mother, father, child or friend can follow, the Name goes with you as your help.
Your line: the name goes too. Today, if you walk someone to a door they must go through alone, a classroom, an interview, a procedure, tell them who goes with them. Day four hundred forty-three.

screen: `DAY 443 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE NAME ON THE HARD ROAD.`

444.title: The Name on the hard road
444.hook: the Name helps on the long road where all else fails (Sukhmani 2)
444.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this stanza within the second ashtpadi, and some return to it during long illnesses, journeys and other hard stretches of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam, and your line: the name goes too. Did you tell someone who goes with them? Today, the road on the other side of that door. Day four hundred forty-four.

A long journey on foot: days of dusty road between towns, no signpost you can trust, no inn guaranteed. Before setting out, a traveler needs a tosaa, a bundle of provisions wrapped in cloth. Nobody sensible leaves without one. Sukhmani's second ashtpadi knows that world. It takes the traveler's bundle, the dark road, the burning sun, the stranger's town, and asks what you'd want with you on the hardest road of all.
screen: `A LONG ROAD ON FOOT.` → `A TOSAA: FOOD WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `WHAT DO YOU TAKE ON THE HARDEST ROAD?`

segments.voice: The stanza is a string of journeys, each with its own danger, and each answered by the Name. In paraphrase: on the road whose miles cannot be counted, the Name of God is your provisions there. On the road of utter darkness, the Name of God is the light with you. On the road where no one knows you, the Name of God is there to recognize you. Where the heat is fierce and the sun burns, the Name of God is your shade. Where thirst torments you, the Name of God rains down like nectar. Count the dangers. Distance. Darkness. Being a stranger. Heat. Thirst. Five dangers, and every one of them gets an answer. The word for provisions is tosaa, the bundle of food from the hook. So the Name is food when the road is too long, light when it's dark, a familiar face in a town of strangers, shade at noon, water when you're parched. Some readers hear this stanza as the journey after death, the road the previous stanza began. Others hear it in life too. A long illness has miles that can't be counted. Depression can be a road of utter darkness. Moving to a new country is a town where no one knows your name. The stanza doesn't say the road will be shortened. It doesn't promise you can skip it. It promises company on it, and provisions for it.
screen: `DISTANCE: THE NAME IS YOUR FOOD.` · `DARKNESS: THE NAME IS YOUR LIGHT.` · `A STRANGE TOWN: THE NAME KNOWS YOU.` · `HEAT AND THIRST: SHADE AND RAIN.` · then, large: `COMPANY ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry one line into a hard task. Think of one hard thing ahead of you today or this week, a long shift, a difficult call, a stretch of caring for someone. Pick the one image from the stanza that fits it best: food for the long road, light in the dark, a known face among strangers, shade, rain. Say that image to yourself slowly, three times. If you pray, add Waheguru. Then breathe with it, and picture yourself walking into the task carrying it like a bundle in cloth. The bell holds the time.
Tosaa, a traveler's provisions: in Sukhmani's second ashtpadi, the Name is food on the endless road, light in the dark, a friend among strangers, shade in the heat, rain in the thirst.
Your line: company on the road. When your hard task begins today, remember the image you packed, and take it out once in the middle. Day four hundred forty-four.

445.title: Living ashtpadi 2
445.hook: the Name as a companion, not a charm
445.howItsDone: Sikhs often read the second ashtpadi of Sukhmani with someone who is ill or grieving, and understand simran as remembering God in company with the Name, not as a spell to change outcomes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tosaa, and your line: company on the road. Did you take your image out in the middle of the hard task? Today, living the second ashtpadi. Day four hundred forty-five.

A lucky coin in a pocket. A charm hanging from a rearview mirror. A phrase muttered before a free throw. People everywhere keep little things that are supposed to make bad stuff not happen. And it's easy to hear the second ashtpadi of Sukhmani that way: say the Name, and the bad thing goes away. But read it again. Not one of its pictures is about the road disappearing. The darkness is still dark. The heat is still hot. The door still shuts. What changes is who's with you.
screen: `A LUCKY COIN, A CHARM, A PHRASE.` → `SAY IT, AND THE BAD THING GOES?` → `READ IT AGAIN: WHO'S WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Gather the second ashtpadi together. The salok: the breaker of the humble's pain, the protector of those with no protector, and Nanak coming to the shelter. The first stanza: where no mother, father, child or friend can go, the Name goes with you. The road stanza: food, light, a known face, shade and rain. All through, the key word is sang, with, together, in company. The Name goes sang, with you. That's the difference between a charm and a companion. A charm is a tool: you use it to get an outcome, and if the outcome doesn't come, the charm failed. A companion is a presence: they don't stop the storm, they sit through it with you. Sikh teaching is wary of using sacred words as magic. Gurbani speaks sharply about empty ritual and outward show, as we'll see in the next ashtpadi, and simran is meant to be remembering, not a spell. So when a Sikh family reads Sukhmani by a hospital bed, the hope is not mainly a bargain, read this and the scan comes back clear. The hope is that the person in the bed, and everyone in the room, isn't alone in what comes. Notice that this makes the Name useful on bad days and good ones alike. A charm is only for emergencies. A companion is for every day: the commute, the kitchen, three in the morning. Never alone isn't a promise that nothing will go wrong. It's a promise about company.
screen: `THE SALOK, THE DOOR, THE ROAD.` · `SANG: WITH YOU, IN COMPANY.` · `A CHARM IS A TOOL; A FRIEND IS PRESENT.` · `FOR BAD DAYS AND GOOD ONES.` · then, large: `NEVER ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember once when alone. Right now, notice that you're alone with this lesson, or alone in your head even if people are near. Instead of filling the quiet, sit in it. Breathe slowly. If you pray, say Waheguru once, not to make anything happen, just to notice company. If you don't, simply notice that this moment is being lived, and you're here in it. Stay with that sense of company for the rest of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Sang, with, together: Sukhmani's second section in daily life, the Name not as a charm that stops the storm, but as a companion who goes with you through it.
Your line: never alone. Today, in one moment you're on your own, a car, a lift, a walk, remember once, not to fix anything, just for the company. Day four hundred forty-five.

446.title: Ashtpadi 3, salok: many scriptures
446.hook: I have searched many scriptures; none equals the Name (Sukhmani 3)
446.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the third ashtpadi; Sikh teachers cite it when speaking of the difference between scholarship and lived remembrance of the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sang, and your line: never alone. Did you remember once, just for the company? Today, the third ashtpadi opens with its salok. Day four hundred forty-six.

Shelves to the ceiling. Notes in every margin. A reader with an answer to every question you could ask. A person like that can teach a great deal. And then there is the other kind of person: someone who has read very little, and yet carries a steadiness the reader doesn't. A grandmother who knew three prayers by heart and lived every one of them. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Arjan, the author of Sukhmani, as the Guru who gathered the hymns of the Adi Granth. And the third ashtpadi opens with a surprising thing for a compiler of scripture to say.
screen: `SHELVES TO THE CEILING.` → `A GRANDMOTHER WITH THREE PRAYERS.` → `A COMPILER OF SCRIPTURE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here is the salok: bahu saasatr bahu simritee pekhe sarab dhadhol. Word by word. Bahu: many. Saasatr: the shastras, the learned treatises of Guru Arjan's world. Simritee: the smritis, the remembered law-books and traditions. Pekhe: I have looked at. Sarab dhadhol: searched through them all. Then the second line: poojas naahee har hare, Naanak naam amol. In paraphrase: they do not equal God, Har, Har; Nanak, the Name is priceless. Amol means beyond price, something no amount of money could buy. Notice who is speaking and how. Not someone who dismisses books without opening them. Someone who says, I have looked, I've searched them all. It's the voice of a scholar, not a scorner. And what he found is that the books point beyond themselves. All that learning can describe the Name, but it can't be the Name. Read this way, the salok isn't against study. The Guru Granth Sahib is itself a book, and Sikhs read from it and sing from it. The salok is about the difference between knowing about God and remembering God. Learning about water is not drinking it. Some readers hear the line as just as true of their own scripture as of any other: reading the Guru Granth Sahib without remembering the One it points to would miss the point too. The salok sets the theme for the whole third ashtpadi. Over the next days its stanzas run through a long list of religious efforts, and set each beside the Name.
screen: `BAHU SAASATR: MANY SCRIPTURES.` · `I HAVE SEARCHED THEM ALL.` · `AMOL: BEYOND PRICE.` · `KNOWING ABOUT VS. REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `NOTHING EQUALS THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line slowly. Choose one line you know, from Sukhmani, from Japji, or from anything that matters to you. If nothing comes, use this: Nanak, the Name is priceless. Say it once at normal speed. Then again, at half speed. Then once more, one word per breath. Notice how the line changes when you stop reading about it and start sitting in it. Let the last word rest. If you pray, add Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Amol, priceless: Sukhmani's third section, whose salok says, I have searched many shastras and smritis, and none equals God; Nanak, the Name is priceless.
Your line: nothing equals the name. Today, when you read or hear something wise, pause before scrolling on, and let one line of it become something you do. Day four hundred forty-six.

447.title: Beyond every pilgrimage
447.hook: pilgrimage, austerity and charity do not equal the Name (Sukhmani 3)
447.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite these stanzas of the third ashtpadi, and Sikh teaching draws on them to stress inner remembrance and honest living over outward ritual.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amol, and your line: nothing equals the name. Did one wise line become something you did? Today, the stanzas that test that claim against every great effort. Day four hundred forty-seven.

You can run a marathon for charity, post the photos, and still be short-tempered with the person who drove you there. You can fast all day and spend it judging everyone who didn't. You can fly across the world to a holy place and bring your worst habits with you in the carry-on. Big effort on the outside, the same old self on the inside. The first stanzas of the third ashtpadi are a long list of big efforts. And they end with a short sentence.
screen: `A MARATHON, A FAST, A FLIGHT.` → `THE SAME SELF IN THE CARRY-ON.` → `A LONG LIST, A SHORT SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here is the list, from the first stanza, in paraphrase. Chanting and austerity, knowledge and every kind of meditation. Expounding the six schools of philosophy and the smritis. The practice of yoga, rituals and religious rites. Renouncing everything and wandering in the forest. Every kind of effort, charity, burnt offerings, gifts of jewels. Cutting the body to pieces and offering it in the fire. Fasts and vows of every sort. And then the short sentence: none of these equal reflecting on the Name of God. Nanak says: through the Guru, chant the Name even once. The next stanza adds the picture behind today's title. In paraphrase: someone longs to die at a place of pilgrimage, and yet pride and ego do not leave the mind. They wash and cleanse themselves day and night, and the dirt of the mind doesn't leave the body. Notice what's being measured. Not whether pilgrimage or fasting are good or bad in themselves. The stanza asks one question of every effort: does it touch the mind? Washing the body isn't washing the mind. A long journey doesn't automatically go inward. Guru Nanak said something like it in Japji: he would bathe at the pilgrimage place, if that pleased the One, and without that, what use is bathing? So the third ashtpadi isn't against effort. It's against effort that skips the inside. The simple, sincere thing done with the whole heart outweighs the grand thing done for show.
screen: `CHANTING, FASTING, THE FOREST, THE FIRE.` · `NONE EQUALS THE NAME.` · `WASHED BODY, UNWASHED MIND.` · `DOES IT TOUCH THE INSIDE?` · then, large: `SIMPLE AND SINCERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do something simple and sincere. Sit for a moment and pick one small thing you can do today with your whole attention. Make a cup of tea for someone and actually look at them when you hand it over. Write two honest lines to a friend. Water a plant slowly. Picture yourself doing it, not for anyone to see, with nothing extra. Then breathe and let the picture settle. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
Teerath, a pilgrimage place: Sukhmani's third ashtpadi says pilgrimage, austerity, ritual and charity do not equal remembering the Name, because washing the body doesn't wash the mind.
Your line: simple and sincere. Today, do the small thing you chose, and do it all the way, with nobody watching. Day four hundred forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 447 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BEST OF ALL WAYS.`

448.title: The best of all ways
448.hook: the highest dharma is to repeat the Name and do pure deeds (Sukhmani 3)
448.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this stanza at the end of the third ashtpadi; its opening line pairs the Name with pure deeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teerath, and your line: simple and sincere. Did you do your small thing all the way? This is a week's end: the breaker of pain, the door, the road, the companion, the many scriptures. Today, what the third ashtpadi puts first. Day four hundred forty-eight.
screen: `SIMPLE AND SINCERE.` · `A WEEK: PAIN BROKEN, THE ROAD, THE SCRIPTURES.`

segments.voice: After a long list of what doesn't measure up, a reader wants to know: so what does? Yesterday's stanzas set fasting, pilgrimage, ritual and learning beside the Name, one by one. If you stopped there, you might think the third ashtpadi was only a list of no. But it ends with a list of yes. The last stanza is built like a ladder of superlatives: of all the ways, this one; of all the efforts, this one; of all the places, this one. And its first rung holds two things together.
screen: `SO WHAT DOES MEASURE UP?` → `A LIST OF NO, THEN A LIST OF YES.` → `A LADDER: OF ALL..., THIS ONE.`

segments.voice: It begins: sarab dharam meh sresht dharam, har ko naam jap nirmal karam. Sarab: all. Dharam: a way of right living, a duty, a practice. Sresht: highest, best. So: of all ways of right living, the highest is to chant the Name of God and do pure deeds. Nirmal means spotless, without dirt. Karam means action. A word about dharam. Here it is read not as a religion, an institution, but as duty, righteousness, the way a person ought to live. So the line isn't a contest between faiths. It's a statement about what a good life is made of: two things, held together. Remembering, and clean action. Then the ladder goes on, in paraphrase. Of all rites, the highest is the company of the holy, which washes away evil thinking. Of all efforts, the best is to chant the Name of God, always. Of all speech, the nectar is to hear God's praise and speak it with your tongue. Of all places, the highest is the heart in which the Name of God dwells. Notice where the ladder ends. Not in a temple. Not on a mountain. In a heart. After all the pilgrimages of yesterday, the best place turns out to be the one you're carrying around. And notice what comes paired with the Name at the very top: nirmal karam, pure deeds. Remembering alone isn't the whole of it. It has to show up in what you do.
screen: `SARAB DHARAM: OF ALL WAYS OF LIVING.` · `THE NAME, AND SPOTLESS ACTION.` · `HOLY COMPANY, GOD'S PRAISE.` · `THE HIGHEST PLACE: A HEART.` · then, large: `NAME AND PURE DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one pure deed. Pure here means clean: no angle, no audience, no score kept. Sit and let one come to mind. Pay a compliment you mean and expect nothing back. Return something you borrowed. Pick up litter no one will thank you for. Fix the thing someone else broke without mentioning it. Choose one, and picture doing it simply. If you pray, say Waheguru once, letting the Name and the deed sit side by side. The bell holds the time.

Dharam, right living: the last stanza of Sukhmani's third ashtpadi says, of all ways of right living, the highest is to chant the Name and do pure deeds, and the highest place is a heart where the Name lives.
Your line: name and pure deeds. Today, do the clean deed you chose, and keep it to yourself. Day four hundred forty-eight.
